notes.front: What is a repeater offset?
notes.back: The difference between a repeater’s transmit and receive frequencies.
notes.explanation: Your radio must use the repeater’s offset, or the repeater will not hear you: an improper offset is one reason you cannot access a repeater.
notes.example: On 2 m a common offset is 600 kHz: the repeater listens 600 kHz above or below the frequency it transmits on.

notes.front: What is the 70 cm band?
notes.back: The UHF amateur band at 420–450 MHz in ITU Region 2, open to Technician and higher licensees.
notes.explanation: Like the 2 m band, its name is its rough wavelength (our calculation from the topic-02 rule of thumb: 300 ÷ 435 MHz ≈ 0.69 m). It has its own common repeater offset, ±5 MHz.
notes.example: The 2 m band is 144–148 MHz (VHF); the 70 cm band, 420–450 MHz, is roughly three times higher in frequency.
notes.source: 47 CFR 97.301(a) (eCFR, current to 2026-09-22); NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T2A03
notes.sourceLicence: B · public domain (US government work, 17 USC 105)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 2026–2030 Technician pool; 47 CFR Part 97 as of 2026-09-22

notes.front: What does simplex operation mean?
notes.back: Transmitting and receiving on the same frequency, station to station, without a repeater.
notes.explanation: Simplex channels let stations within range of each other talk without tying up a repeater.
notes.example: Two hikers on the same 2 m frequency talking handheld to handheld, instead of through a repeater with an offset.

notes.front: What is a band plan, beyond the privileges the FCC sets?
notes.back: A voluntary guideline for using different modes or activities within an amateur band.
notes.explanation: FCC rules say what you may do; band plans say where amateurs agree to do it, such as repeater and simplex frequencies.
notes.example: Band plans set aside frequencies such as the 2 m simplex calling frequency, 146.520 MHz; the pool's syllabus lists calling frequencies and repeater offsets under band plans.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T2A10, T2A02 and syllabus T2A
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 2026–2030 Technician pool; 47 CFR Part 97 as of 2026-09-22

notes.front: What does the procedural signal “CQ” mean?
notes.back: Calling any station.
notes.explanation: You use it to invite a contact from anyone listening, rather than a particular station.
notes.example: “CQ CQ CQ, this is KL7CC” invites any station to reply, unlike calling one station by its call sign.

notes.front: What does a receiver’s squelch function do?
notes.back: It mutes the receiver audio when a signal is not present.
notes.explanation: Squelch keeps the speaker quiet between transmissions; set too tight, it can also hide a weak signal.
notes.example: Your handheld stays silent while the channel is empty, then opens when a station transmits.

notes.front: What is CTCSS?
notes.back: A sub-audible tone sent along with normal voice audio to open a receiver’s squelch (Continuous Tone-Coded Squelch System).
notes.explanation: A repeater that expects a CTCSS tone ignores you if you send the wrong one.
notes.example: Like a key only the right tone turns: with the correct tone set, the repeater hears you; without it, it stays shut.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T2B02, T8C06, T2B04

notes.front: What is DTMF signalling?
notes.back: Signalling to a repeater using two simultaneous audio tones (Dual-Tone Multi-Frequency).
notes.explanation: The pool lists it with CTCSS as a repeater access tone; later you will see it used to reach linked systems over the internet.
notes.example: Unlike CTCSS, a single sub-audible tone sent with your voice, DTMF sends two audio tones at once.

notes.front: What is the reverse function on a VHF/UHF transceiver for?
notes.back: To listen on a repeater’s input frequency.
notes.explanation: A repeater listens on one frequency and transmits on another; reverse, on a VHF/UHF transceiver (a combined transmitter and receiver), lets you hear the one it listens on.
notes.example: Normally you hear the repeater’s output; pressing reverse lets you hear stations transmitting to the repeater.

image.alt: Diagram: your radio transmits to the repeater on the repeater’s input frequency; the repeater retransmits on its output frequency. The offset is the difference between the two frequencies. The reverse function lets you listen on the input.
image.credit: Drawn for this deck from NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T2A07 and T2B01

notes.front: What is a linked repeater network?
notes.back: A network of repeaters in which signals received by one repeater are transmitted by all the repeaters in the network.
notes.explanation: Linking extends coverage far beyond one repeater’s range.
notes.example: You talk into a local repeater and stations near every other repeater in the network hear you.

notes.front: What are Q signals?
notes.back: Short codes beginning with Q that stand for set messages, such as QRM (interference from other stations) and QSY (changing frequency).
notes.explanation: They save words on the air; the pool asks about QRM and QSY.
notes.example: Saying “QSY” instead of “I am changing frequency”.

notes.front: What is DMR?
notes.back: A technique for time-multiplexing two digital voice signals on a single 12.5 kHz repeater channel.
notes.explanation: Time-multiplexing means the two signals take turns in rapid time slots, so one 12.5 kHz-wide channel carries two conversations. DMR also uses its own settings, such as talkgroups and color codes.
notes.example: Unlike an FM repeater, which carries one voice signal, one DMR repeater channel carries two digital voice signals.

notes.front: What is a DMR talkgroup?
notes.back: An identifier DMR uses to organise radio traffic, so those who want to hear the group are not bothered by other traffic.
notes.explanation: You join a talkgroup by programming your radio with the group’s ID or code.
notes.example: Like a chat channel: you hear the talkgroup you selected, not everyone on the network.

notes.front: What is the digital color code on a DMR repeater system?
notes.back: An access code that must be programmed into a DMR transmitter to access a specific repeater.
notes.explanation: Without the right color code, the DMR repeater will not let you in.
notes.example: The color code opens a specific repeater; the talkgroup then picks whose traffic you hear on it.

notes.front: A common repeater offset in the 2 m band is plus or minus {{c1::600 kHz}}.
notes.explanation: The pool cites no FCC rule for this: it is common practice.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 2026–2030 Technician pool; 47 CFR Part 97 as of 2026-09-22

notes.front: A common repeater offset in the 70 cm band is plus or minus {{c1::5 MHz}}.
notes.explanation: The higher band uses the larger offset: 5 MHz on 70 cm against 600 kHz on 2 m.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 2026–2030 Technician pool; 47 CFR Part 97 as of 2026-09-22

notes.front: The national calling frequency for FM simplex in the 2 m band is {{c1::146.520 MHz}}.
notes.explanation: It is where you call to find someone on simplex; the pool cites no FCC rule for it.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 2026–2030 Technician pool; 47 CFR Part 97 as of 2026-09-22

notes.front: On a repeater, how do you call a station whose call sign you know?
notes.back: Say their call sign, then identify with your own.
notes.explanation: No “CQ” or “break, break” is needed; the station you want hears their call sign first.

notes.front: How do you answer a station calling CQ?
notes.back: Send the other station’s call sign, followed by your own.
notes.explanation: The same order as calling any known station: their call sign first, then yours.

notes.front: Off a repeater, how do you effectively seek a call from any phone station?
notes.back: Repeat “CQ” a few times, then “this is” and your call sign; pause to listen, and repeat as necessary.
notes.explanation: Pausing gives stations a chance to answer before you call again.

notes.front: What is the customary way to show you are listening on a repeater and looking for a contact?
notes.back: Give your call sign followed by the word “listening”.
notes.explanation: On repeaters this replaces calling CQ.

notes.front: You can hear a repeater’s output but cannot access it. What could be wrong?
notes.back: Any of: an improper offset, the wrong CTCSS tone, or the wrong DCS (Digital-Coded Squelch) code.
notes.explanation: The repeater must hear you on its input frequency, with the access tone or code it expects: a CTCSS tone, or a DCS code, the other kind of access code the pool lists.

notes.front: What would cause your FM audio to drop out on voice peaks?
notes.back: Talking too loudly.
notes.explanation: The pool keys talking too loudly. For an FM transceiver that is over-deviating, its frequency swinging further than it should, the pool's cure is to talk farther from the microphone. (Deviation is how far the frequency swings; 47 CFR 2.202(g) defines peak deviation as half the difference between the highest and lowest instantaneous frequency.)
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T2B05, T7B01; 47 CFR 2.202(g) (eCFR, current to 2026-09-22)

notes.front: How do you join a digital repeater’s talkgroup?
notes.back: Program your radio with the group’s ID or code.
notes.explanation: On a DMR radio you select a group by entering its identification code.

notes.front: Two stations on the same frequency interfere with each other. What applies?
notes.back: The stations should negotiate continued use of the frequency.
notes.explanation: No frequency is assigned for any station's exclusive use, and each station licensee and control operator must cooperate in selecting channels (97.101(b)); so neither station has a prior claim, and they should agree.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T2B08; 47 CFR 97.101(b) (eCFR, current to 2026-09-22)

notes.front: Why do VHF/UHF band plans designate simplex channels?
notes.back: So stations within range of each other can communicate without tying up a repeater.
notes.explanation: The repeater stays free for stations that need it to reach each other.

notes.front: The Q signal {{c1::QRM}} means you are receiving interference from other stations.
notes.explanation: QRM and QRN look alike; for interference from other stations the pool keys QRM, and QRN is its distractor.

notes.front: The Q signal {{c1::QSY}} means you are changing frequency.
notes.explanation: Q signals stand for set messages; QSY is the one for changing frequency, and the pool also uses it as a wrong answer when asking how to show you are listening on a repeater.

notes.front: How do you set the squelch so that a weak FM signal can be heard?
notes.back: Set the squelch threshold so the receiver audio is on all the time.
notes.explanation: A weak signal may not open the squelch, so you open it fully and listen through the noise.

notes.front: What is a common repeater frequency offset in the 2-meter band?
notes.back: Plus or minus 600 kHz
notes.choices:
A) Plus or minus 5 MHz
B) Plus or minus 600 kHz
C) Plus or minus 500 kHz
D) Plus or minus 1 MHz
notes.choicesExplained: A: ±5 MHz is the common 70 cm offset. C: ±500 kHz is not the common 2 m offset. D: ±1 MHz is not the common 2 m offset.
notes.explanation: 600 kHz goes with 2 m (144–148 MHz); ±5 MHz, offered here as a distractor, is the common offset in the higher 70 cm band. The pool cites no rule: the syllabus lists repeater offsets under band plans.

notes.front: What is the national calling frequency for FM simplex operations in the 2-meter band?
notes.choicesExplained: B: 145.000 MHz is in the 2 m band but is not the calling frequency. C: 432.100 MHz is in the 70 cm band (420–450 MHz). D: 446.000 MHz is in the 70 cm band, not 2 m.
notes.explanation: Band plans set calling frequencies, and 146.520 MHz is the one for 2 m FM simplex; the pool cites no FCC rule for it. 432.100 and 446.000 MHz are in the 70 cm band, not 2 m.

notes.front: What is a common repeater frequency offset in the 70-centimeter band?
notes.back: Plus or minus 5 MHz
notes.choices:
A) Plus or minus 5 MHz
B) Plus or minus 600 kHz
C) Plus or minus 500 kHz
D) Plus or minus 1 MHz
notes.choicesExplained: B: ±600 kHz is the common 2 m offset. C: ±500 kHz is not the common 70 cm offset. D: ±1 MHz is not the common 70 cm offset.
notes.explanation: The two common offsets are swapped as distractors: ±600 kHz belongs to 2 m; ±5 MHz belongs to the higher-frequency 70 cm band (420–450 MHz).

notes.front: What is an appropriate way to call another station on a repeater if you know the other station's call sign?
notes.back: Say the station's call sign, then identify with your call sign
notes.choices:
A) Say "break, break," then the other station’s call sign, followed by your call sign
B) Say the station's call sign, then identify with your call sign
C) Say "CQ" three times, then the other station's call sign, followed by your call sign
D) Wait for the station to call CQ, then answer with your call sign
notes.choicesExplained: A: “break, break” is not how you call a known station. C: CQ is for calling any station, not a known one. D: you need not wait for a CQ to call a station you know.
notes.explanation: You already know whom you want, so you name that station first, then give your own call sign to identify yourself. CQ is for calling any station, so it is not needed here.

notes.front: How should you respond to a station calling CQ?
notes.back: Transmit the other station’s call sign followed by your call sign
notes.choices:
A) Transmit "CQ" followed by the other station’s call sign
B) Transmit your call sign followed by the other station’s call sign
C) Transmit the other station’s call sign followed by your call sign
D) Transmit a signal report followed by your call sign
notes.choicesExplained: A: you do not send CQ when answering one. B: the order is reversed: their call sign comes first. D: a signal report does not replace their call sign.
notes.explanation: The calling station is listening for replies, so it hears its own call sign first and then learns from yours who is answering. It is the same order as calling a known station.

notes.front: What is an effective way to seek a call from any phone station when not using a repeater?
notes.back: Repeat “CQ” a few times, followed by “this is,” and your call sign, then pause to listen; repeat as necessary
notes.choices:
A) Sign your call sign once, followed by the words “listening for a call;” if there is no answer, change the frequency and repeat
B) Say “QTC,” followed by “this is” and your call sign; if there is no answer, change the frequency and repeat
C) Transmit an unmodulated carrier for approximately 10 seconds, followed by “this is” and your call sign, and pause to listen; repeat as necessary
D) Repeat “CQ” a few times, followed by “this is,” and your call sign, then pause to listen; repeat as necessary
notes.choicesExplained: A: this resembles the repeater custom; off a repeater, the keyed method is calling CQ a few times. B: QTC is not the general call to any station; CQ is. C: an unmodulated carrier is not a call; the keyed method uses CQ.
notes.explanation: CQ means calling any station, so repeating it a few times and then giving your call sign tells listeners who wants a contact; pausing gives them a chance to answer. Call sign plus “listening” is the repeater custom instead.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T2A06, T2A09, T2A08

notes.front: What does the term "repeater offset" mean?
notes.back: The difference between a repeater’s transmit and receive frequencies
notes.choices:
A) The difference between a repeater’s transmit and receive frequencies
B) The repeater has a time delay to prevent interference
C) The approximately half-second delay to allow for the “squelch tail” to be removed
D) The fee charged by the repeater owner or club to provide for maintenance
notes.choicesExplained: B: the offset is a frequency difference, not a time delay. C: a squelch tail delay is not the offset. D: the offset is not a fee.
notes.explanation: A repeater retransmits another station's signal on a different channel (47 CFR 97.3(a)(40)), so it receives on one frequency and transmits on another; the difference between the two is the offset, a frequency and not a delay or a fee.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T2A07; 47 CFR 97.3(a)(40) (eCFR, current to 2026-09-22)

image.alt: Diagram: your radio transmits to the repeater on the repeater’s input frequency; the repeater retransmits on its output frequency. The offset is the difference between the two frequencies. The reverse function lets you listen on the input.
image.credit: Drawn for this deck from NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T2A07 and T2B01

notes.front: What is the meaning of the procedural signal “CQ”?
notes.back: Calling any station
notes.choices:
A) A shortened form of the term “Contest QSO”
B) “Communication Quality,” used to indicate transmitted audio clarity
C) Only the called station should transmit
D) Calling any station
notes.choicesExplained: A: CQ is not short for “Contest QSO”. B: CQ does not mean “Communication Quality”. C: CQ invites any station, not only a called one.
notes.explanation: CQ is the general call: you use it when you want a contact with anyone listening, not a particular station, and a station that hears it answers with your call sign then its own.

notes.front: Which of the following is a customary way to indicate a station is listening on a repeater and looking for a contact?
notes.back: The station’s call sign followed by the word “listening”
notes.choices:
A) “CQ CQ” followed by the repeater’s call sign
B) The station’s call sign followed by the word “listening”
C) The repeater’s call sign followed by the station’s call sign
D) “QSY” followed by your call sign
notes.choicesExplained: A: calling CQ with the repeater’s call sign is not the repeater custom. C: the repeater’s call sign is not needed. D: QSY means changing frequency.
notes.explanation: Your call sign plus “listening” is the repeater custom the pool keys; calling CQ a few times is the method it keys off a repeater, and QSY means changing frequency.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T2A09, T2A06, T2B11

notes.front: What is a band plan, beyond the privileges established by the FCC?
notes.back: A voluntary guideline for using different modes or activities within an amateur band
notes.choices:
A) A voluntary guideline for using different modes or activities within an amateur band
B) A list of operating schedules
C) A list of available net frequencies
D) A plan devised by a club to indicate frequency band usage
notes.choicesExplained: B: operating schedules are not a band plan. C: a list of net frequencies is not a band plan. D: a band plan is not one club’s private plan.
notes.explanation: The FCC sets the privileges; a band plan goes further by voluntary agreement, sorting modes and activities within a band, such as the simplex channels in VHF/UHF band plans. It is not one club's own plan.

notes.front: What term describes an amateur station that is transmitting and receiving on the same frequency?
notes.back: Simplex
notes.choices:
A) Full duplex
B) Diplex
C) Simplex
D) Multiplex
notes.choicesExplained: A: full duplex is not the term for one shared frequency. B: diplex is not the term for one shared frequency. D: multiplex is not the term for one shared frequency.
notes.explanation: “Simplex” is the term for one shared frequency; a repeater, by contrast, receives and transmits on frequencies separated by the offset.

notes.front: What is the purpose of the reverse function on a VHF/UHF transceiver?
notes.back: To listen on a repeater’s input frequency
notes.choices:
A) To reduce power output
B) To increase power output
C) To listen on a repeater’s input frequency
D) To listen on a repeater’s output frequency
notes.choicesExplained: A: reverse does not change power. B: reverse does not change power. D: you already hear the output normally; reverse is for the input.
notes.explanation: You normally hear a repeater's output. Reverse sets your transceiver (a combined transmitter and receiver) to listen on the repeater's input frequency instead, so you hear stations transmitting to the repeater.

image.alt: Diagram: your radio transmits to the repeater on the repeater’s input frequency; the repeater retransmits on its output frequency. The offset is the difference between the two frequencies. The reverse function lets you listen on the input.
image.credit: Drawn for this deck from NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T2A07 and T2B01

notes.front: What term describes the use of a sub-audible tone transmitted along with normal voice audio to open the squelch of a receiver?
notes.back: CTCSS
notes.choices:
A) Carrier squelch
B) Tone burst
C) DTMF
D) CTCSS
notes.choicesExplained: A: carrier squelch is not a tone system; the tone system is CTCSS. B: a tone burst is not the continuous sub-audible tone asked about. C: DTMF uses two simultaneous audible tones, not a sub-audible one.
notes.explanation: Continuous Tone-Coded Squelch System: the tone is continuous and sub-audible, sent with your voice, and the receiver's squelch opens only for it. That is why a repeater ignores you if you send the wrong CTCSS tone.

notes.front: Which of the following describes a linked repeater network?
notes.back: A network of repeaters in which signals received by one repeater are transmitted by all the repeaters in the network
notes.choices:
A) A network of repeaters in which signals received by one repeater are transmitted by all the repeaters in the network
B) A single repeater with more than one receiver
C) Multiple repeaters with the same control operator
D) A system of repeaters linked by APRS
notes.choicesExplained: B: one repeater with several receivers is not a network. C: sharing a control operator does not link the signals. D: APRS (Automatic Packet Reporting System, taught in topic 13) linking is not what defines the network; retransmission by every repeater is.
notes.explanation: Linking is about signals: what one repeater receives, all the repeaters in the network transmit, so a station near any of them hears you.

notes.front: Which of the following could be the reason you are unable to access a repeater whose output you can hear?
notes.back: All these choices are correct
notes.choices:
A) Improper transceiver offset
B) You are using the wrong CTCSS tone
C) You are using the wrong DCS code
D) All these choices are correct
notes.choicesExplained: A: correct, but so are B and C. B: correct, but so are A and C. C: correct, but so are A and B.
notes.explanation: An improper offset, the wrong CTCSS tone or the wrong DCS (Digital-Coded Squelch) code each stops the repeater hearing you: it listens on its input frequency and waits for the access tone or code it expects.

notes.front: Which of the following would cause your FM transmission audio to drop out on voice peaks?
notes.back: You are talking too loudly
notes.choices:
A) Your repeater offset is inverted
B) Your FM deviation is too low
C) You are talking too loudly
D) Your transmit power is too high
notes.choicesExplained: A: an inverted offset stops you reaching the repeater at all. B: too little deviation (how far the FM frequency swings) is not the keyed cause; the pool's cure for over-deviation, talking farther from the microphone, points the other way. D: transmit power does not cause audio dropout on peaks.
notes.explanation: The pool keys talking too loudly; for an FM transceiver that is over-deviating, it keys talking farther away from the microphone.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T2B05, T7B01; 47 CFR 2.202(g) (eCFR, current to 2026-09-22)

notes.front: What type of signaling to a repeater uses two simultaneous audio tones?
notes.back: DTMF
notes.choices:
A) DTMF
B) CTCSS
C) GMRS
D) D-STAR
notes.choicesExplained: B: CTCSS is a single sub-audible tone. C: GMRS (General Mobile Radio Service) is a separate two-way voice service under Part 95 of the FCC rules (47 CFR 95.1703), not a signalling method. D: D-STAR is a digital system (the pool speaks of a “D-STAR digital transceiver”), not two-tone signalling.
notes.explanation: DTMF stands for Dual-Tone Multi-Frequency: each signal is two audio tones at once. CTCSS, by contrast, is one sub-audible tone.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T2B06, T2B02, T4B11; 47 CFR 95.1703 (eCFR, current to 2026-09-22)

notes.front: How can you join a digital repeater’s “talkgroup”?
notes.back: Program your radio with the group’s ID or code
notes.choices:
A) Register with the local Frequency Coordinator
B) Register with the digital repeater control operator
C) Program your radio with the group’s ID or code
D) Program your radio with the DTMF tone used by the talkgroup
notes.choicesExplained: A: the frequency coordinator recommends repeater channels; it does not manage talkgroups. B: no registration is needed; you program the ID. D: talkgroups are selected by ID, not by DTMF tone.
notes.explanation: A talkgroup is an identifier, so a radio joins one by being programmed with that ID or code; a group on a DMR radio is likewise selected by entering its identification code.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T2B07, T2B14, T4B09

notes.front: Which of the following applies when two stations transmitting on the same frequency interfere with each other?
notes.back: The stations should negotiate continued use of the frequency
notes.choices:
A) The stations should negotiate continued use of the frequency
B) Both stations should choose another frequency to avoid conflict
C) Whichever station was on the frequency first has preemptive rights to the frequency
D) Use subaudible tones so both stations can share the frequency
notes.choicesExplained: B: the rule asks stations to cooperate in choosing channels (97.101(b)), not for both to leave. C: being first gives no preemptive right: no frequency is assigned for any station's exclusive use. D: sub-audible tones do not let two signals share a frequency.
notes.explanation: No frequency is assigned for the exclusive use of any station, and licensees and control operators must cooperate in selecting channels (97.101(b)), so the stations should work it out between them.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T2B08; 47 CFR 97.101(b) (eCFR, current to 2026-09-22)

notes.front: Why are simplex channels designated in the VHF/UHF band plans?
notes.back: So stations within range of each other can communicate without tying up a repeater
notes.choices:
A) So stations within range of each other can communicate without tying up a repeater
B) For contest operation
C) For working DX only
D) So stations with simple transmitters can access the repeater without automated offset
notes.choicesExplained: B: simplex channels are not for contests. C: they are not for working distant (DX) stations only. D: simplex does not access a repeater at all.
notes.explanation: Stations within range of each other do not need a repeater, so talking on a simplex channel leaves the repeater free for stations that do.

notes.front: Which Q signal indicates that you are receiving interference from other stations?
notes.back: QRM
notes.choices:
A) QRM
B) QRN
C) QTH
D) QSB
notes.choicesExplained: B: QRN looks like QRM, but it is not the pool's answer for interference from other stations. C: QTH does not mean interference. D: QSB does not mean interference.
notes.explanation: Q signals stand for set messages, so each must be learned; for interference from other stations the pool keys QRM.

notes.front: Which Q signal indicates that you are changing frequency?
notes.back: QSY
notes.choices:
A) QRU
B) QSY
C) QSL
D) QRZ
notes.choicesExplained: A: QRU does not mean changing frequency. C: QSL does not mean changing frequency. D: QRZ does not mean changing frequency.
notes.explanation: Q signals stand for set messages; QSY is the one for changing frequency, and the pool uses it as a wrong answer elsewhere too.

notes.front: What is the digital color code used on DMR repeater systems?
notes.back: An access code which must be programmed into a DMR transmitter to access a specific repeater
notes.choices:
A) An access code which must be programmed into a DMR transmitter to access a specific repeater
B) A code which automatically programs the repeater offset to a frequency chosen by the user
C) A code which identifies the specific CODEC being used so that the repeater can properly decode the audio
D) A code transmitted by the repeater to indicate health and status of the equipment
notes.choicesExplained: B: it does not set the repeater offset. C: it does not identify the CODEC (the coder-decoder that turns voice into digital data). D: it is not a health or status signal.
notes.explanation: A DMR repeater expects its color code, so without it programmed your transmitter cannot access that repeater; the talkgroup then sorts the traffic you hear.

notes.front: What is the purpose of a squelch function?
notes.back: Mute the receiver audio when a signal is not present
notes.choices:
A) Reduce a CW transmitter's key clicks
B) Mute the receiver audio when a signal is not present
C) Eliminate parasitic oscillations in an RF amplifier
D) Reduce interference from impulse noise
notes.choicesExplained: A: key clicks come from a CW transmitter, as the choice says; squelch is a receiver function. C: parasitic oscillations are an RF amplifier problem, not receiver audio. D: squelch only mutes the audio when no signal is present, so it does nothing about impulse noise heard while you listen to a signal.
notes.explanation: Squelch keeps the receiver quiet between transmissions by muting the audio when no signal is present; open it fully and the audio is on all the time.

notes.front: Which of the following is a “talkgroup”?
notes.back: An identifier used by DMR to organize radio traffic so that those who want to hear the group aren’t bothered by other radio traffic
notes.choices:
A) A group of amateur radio operators who share email on a specific amateur radio topic
B) An identifier used by DMR to organize radio traffic so that those who want to hear the group aren’t bothered by other radio traffic
C) The members of a net organized for amateur radio operators with a specific common interest
D) A method of automatically alerting all group members to the frequency where any member is transmitting
notes.choicesExplained: A: an email group is not a talkgroup. C: net members are a net, not a DMR talkgroup. D: a talkgroup does not alert members to frequencies.
notes.explanation: Many conversations share a DMR network, so the talkgroup identifier sorts the traffic: you hear the group you want and are not bothered by the rest.

notes.front: How is squelch adjusted so that a weak FM signal can be heard?
notes.back: Set the squelch threshold so that receiver output audio is on all the time
notes.choices:
A) Set the squelch threshold so that receiver output audio is on all the time
B) Turn up the audio level until it overcomes the squelch threshold
C) Turn on the anti-squelch function
D) Enable squelch enhancement
notes.choicesExplained: B: volume does not change the squelch threshold. C and D: “anti-squelch” and “squelch enhancement” are not the answer: a weak signal may not open the squelch, so you lower the threshold until the audio stays on.
notes.explanation: A weak signal may not be strong enough to open the squelch, so you set the threshold so the audio is on all the time and listen for it.

notes.front: How is a specific group of stations selected on a DMR digital voice transceiver?
notes.back: By entering the group’s identification code
notes.choices:
A) By retrieving the frequencies from transceiver memory
B) By enabling the group’s CTCSS tone
C) By entering the group’s identification code
D) By inserting a five-pin, pre-programmed code plug
notes.choicesExplained: A: frequencies alone do not select a group. B: CTCSS tones do not select DMR groups. D: a code plug is configuration data loaded onto the radio, not a physical plug.
notes.explanation: A DMR group is chosen by its identification code, just as you join a talkgroup by programming its ID; on a DMR transceiver (a combined transmitter and receiver), frequencies or CTCSS tones do not pick a group.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T4B09, T4B07, T2B07

notes.front: How does CTCSS differ from DTMF?
notes.back: CTCSS is one sub-audible tone sent with your voice to open squelch; DTMF is two simultaneous audio tones used for signalling.
notes.explanation: Both are ways of talking to a repeater, which is why they are easy to confuse.

notes.front: How does a DMR color code differ from a talkgroup?
notes.back: The color code is an access code for a specific repeater; the talkgroup organises traffic into the group you want to hear.
notes.explanation: You need the right color code to get into the repeater, then the talkgroup chooses the conversation.

notes.front: Which common repeater offset goes with which band: 600 kHz or 5 MHz?
notes.back: 2 m: ±600 kHz. 70 cm: ±5 MHz.
notes.explanation: The two numbers are swapped as distractors in the pool.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 2026–2030 Technician pool; 47 CFR Part 97 as of 2026-09-22

notes.front: How does simplex differ from working through a repeater?
notes.back: Simplex: both stations transmit and receive on one frequency. Repeater: it receives and transmits on frequencies separated by the offset.
notes.explanation: Simplex needs the stations to be in range of each other; the repeater extends range but is shared.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T2A11, T2A07, T2B09

notes.front: QRM or QSY: which means interference and which means changing frequency?
notes.back: QRM: interference from other stations. QSY: changing frequency.
notes.explanation: Both are Q signals in the pool, and QSY also turns up there as a wrong answer about repeater calling.
notes.source: NCVEC 2026–2030 Technician Pool, T2B10, T2B11, T2A09
